Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00867

We answer: have you not heard God's words in the chapter The All-Merciful: “The heaven He raised, and He set the balance. Weigh with justice, and do not fall short in the balance”? Have you not heard what He says in Iron: “We sent Our messengers with clear signs, and sent down with them the Book and the balance, so that people might uphold justice”? Do you think, thoughtful reader, that the balance God sent down with the Book and His messengers is only a device for weighing barley, wheat, rice, and dates? Do you think the balance set beside the heavens is a steelyard or a balance for weighing? That is a far-fetched mistake, and a shameful misrepresentation. Take care, reader, when interpreting the meanings of the Book. Do not force them, or stubbornly follow ignorance. I warn you not to be among the ignorant.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00868

Know that what leads people like you—those who read the words of the Qur'an and the Prophet only in their everyday, outward sense—to take them as referring to ordinary things is their inability to think beyond bodies and physical things. If they would pause to consider the meaning of “balance,” and set aside the extra details and special shapes people associate with it, they would see that a balance does not have to have a particular shape or be a physical object. At its heart, a balance is anything by which one thing is measured against another. The things measured need not be physical. A steelyard or a two-pan balance measures weight; an astrolabe measures heights and times; a plumb line tests whether a column is upright; a ruler checks whether a line is straight. In the same way, logic measures reasoning in the theoretical sciences and shows sound thought from unsound thought. Grammar measures how words are formed; prosody measures poetry; the senses measure some things we perceive; and complete reason is a measure for everything. In short, the measure for each thing must be of the same kind as the thing measured.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00869

The balance mentioned in the Qur'an should therefore be understood as the noblest of all balances: the balance of the Day of Reckoning. It is the measure of knowledge and of the deeds of the heart that grow out of bodily actions. When Ja'far al-Sadiq was asked about God's words, “We will set up the just scales,” he said, “The scales are the prophets and the saints.” The scale of the afterlife is what lets us recognize things as they really are: knowledge of God, His highest qualities and greatest works, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day and Resurrection—as taught by God's prophets, who learned from the angels, who learned from God. The first teacher is God, the second is Gabriel, and the third is the Messenger.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00870

God sent down from heaven five measures, drawn from the Qur'an, so that each person can know the extent of their knowledge and reason, and can measure their effort and deeds. They are the measure of equality, the measure of entailment, and the measure of contradiction. The measure of equality has three forms: the greater, the middle, and the lesser. Together these make five. We explain their details, each form, and how to draw them from the Qur'an in our book The Keys to the Unseen. In truth, they are ladders by which the spirit rises toward the heavens and toward nearness to the Source of all things. The steps and principles set out there are stages on the spiritual ascent. A bodily ascent is beyond the power of most souls; it belongs only to the soul of the Prophet. In short, these measures of the afterlife let us weigh thoughts and judge insights in the true sciences, which are spiritual provisions for the people of the next life.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00871

God sent them down from heaven so each person can know the extent of their knowledge and reason, measure their effort and deeds, and reckon their provision, their appointed term, the record of their life, and their hopes. Every creature has a particular provision, a known term, a written limit, and an account. Spiritual provisions, like bodily provisions, differ in kind and amount, and in how long they sustain life, how they benefit, and how they harm. The provisions of the afterlife differ even more than those of this world. God says, “The Hereafter has greater ranks and greater distinctions.” He also tells His Prophet, who warned and taught the people, “Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good counsel, and debate with them in the best way.” He commands the Prophet to offer different forms of spiritual provision to people, according to their different natures and dispositions. The Qur'an is like a table sent down from heaven to earth, spread with different kinds of food. Each group has its allotted provision and share of life. Wisdom and proof are food for some, counsel and public teaching for others, and debate and the appeal to common opinion for another group.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00872

The Qur'an also contains food for other groups that is less subtle: it is like husks and bran, suited to people whose natures are coarse and low. As God says, “There is nothing fresh or dry that is not in a clear Book.” Just as it contains the nourishment of sound reason for people of understanding, so it contains something like straw and husks for ordinary people, whose rank is like that of cattle. God says, “As a provision for you and your cattle.” Food must resemble the one who eats it. What is sensed nourishes the power of sensation; imagined or supposed things nourish the imaginative and estimating powers; and intelligible things nourish the intellect. Through them, the intellect is fed and strengthened, reaches its full development, and moves from a state of potential understanding to the active intellect, where it remains forever.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00873
1. A note on the scales
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00874

One thing a traveler on the road to the afterlife must understand is how to compare the two worlds and weigh what exists in one against what exists in the other. If God opens the heart to compare the visible world with the hidden world, it becomes easier to follow God's path and enter the Abode of Peace. The traveler will learn many of the Qur'an's secrets and levels, and see the realities and lights in its verses—things missed by most scholars who rely on formal learning and by famous philosophers who are thought to be wise. This is a great opening into the true nature of things, especially the afterlife. It is also the first stage of prophecy. The prophets first begin to see in dreams what is in the spiritual world. The realities of things appear to them dressed in imagined forms, because a true dream is one part of prophecy.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00875

Realities do not appear without the clothing of an image until the world of Resurrection, where they exist on their own. In this world they are covered by sensory, material forms. The same is true in a true dream and in the world between death and Resurrection, though there the covering is thinner: realities appear in imagined forms. Whoever learns to compare these worlds—or the three worlds—will understand how to interpret sayings and dreams. Dreams are part of prophecy because they let the dreamer see what is in that world without the usual coverings. This ability belongs to the prophets while they are still human, but other saints gain it only after leaving this life.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00876

Reflect on this, dear friend. Perhaps a window into the spiritual world will open for you. Otherwise, you will remain turned toward the coverings of animal habit and imitation, drawing your attention away from the lights of the spiritual world and relying on sensation and imitation. Then none of the hidden wisdom or secrets of the Resurrection will be revealed to you.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00877

Know that you are traveling from this world to the next. Your life in this world is your capital; your trade is the knowledge you acquire, your provision for the journey; your profit is eternal life and the joy of meeting God and entering His spiritual realm. Your loss is the destruction of your soul through being kept from nearness to God and the Abode of His honor. Know that the judge sees clearly and accepts only pure gold—the knowledge and obedience that are free of dross. Weigh your good deeds with a true balance that does not tilt. Take account of yourself before your life ends and you are judged at a time when nothing can be set right. The scales are set up for the Day of Reckoning, when reward and punishment are given. Those whose scales are heavy will live in contentment; those whose scales are light will fall into the Abyss. “How will you know what it is? A blazing Fire.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00878

As for the measure of deeds, every bodily action has an effect on the soul. Good deeds and acts of worship—prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, almsgiving, struggle, and the like—light up the soul, free it from the grip of desire, cleanse it of the darkness of bodily matter, and draw it from this world to the next and from the lower abode to the higher one. Each good deed has a particular effect in bringing light and purification. As good deeds multiply, their effects and light grow. Each bad deed likewise has a particular power to darken and cloud the soul, bind it to this world and its desires, and fetter it with chains. As sins multiply, darkness and heaviness grow stronger.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00879

These effects remain hidden from people in this world. When the Hour comes and the veils are lifted, the truth will become clear. Each person will find the measure of their own effort and deeds, and see which side of the scale is heavier—the light of their obedience or the darkness of their rejection. In short, during life each person performs many separate deeds: good, bad, or mixed. On the Day of Resurrection, when the total of these deeds is brought together, one side may outweigh the other, or the two may be equal. If the good deeds outweigh the bad, the person will be among the blessed; if the bad outweigh the good, they will be among the wretched. If the two are equal, the person will stand between the two groups until God decides whether to punish them or show them mercy. But mercy is more likely, since God is the Giver without limit.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00880

These three groups are judged according to their deeds. But there is another group, higher than all the rest: those whose whole being is absorbed in witnessing God's majesty. They pay no attention to good or bad deeds. They have broken the two pans of their scales and left behind the world of deeds and measures, with its balance and extremes. They have entered the world of knowledge and inner states, and gaze on the lights of beauty and majesty.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00881

In the beginning, then, everyone whose certainty, faith, and affirmation of God's oneness have not freed them from the chains of nature and the power of this world remains bound to their deeds. They are like a two-pan balance, pulled in opposite directions by the results of their actions. One pan tilts downward toward Hell according to the amount of passing worldly goods in it. The other tilts upward toward the Abode of Bliss according to the amount of afterlife provision it holds. On the Great Day of Gathering, when the two pans pull in opposite directions, God, the Most High and Great, will decide which abode each person enters, according to which pan is heavier.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00882

The pan of good deeds is on the right, the eastern side; the pan of bad deeds is on the left, the western side. Once one side outweighs the other and judgment is carried out, the two pans become, in effect, one. The winning side overcomes and erases the other. The blessed will have both hands on the right; the people of the left will have both hands on the left. Understand this.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00883
XXII. Groups of people on the Day of Resurrection
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00884

As you have learned, people in the next life fall into three broad groups: those brought near to God, the blessed people of the right, and the wretched people of the left. In terms of their final reckoning, they fall into two main classes. The first class enters Paradise and receives its blessings without an account. It contains three groups.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00885

The first group is made up of those brought near to God, who have reached perfection in knowledge and freedom from worldly ties. Their high station and freedom from the concerns of books and accounts allow them to enter Paradise without being called to account. God says of people like them, “You are not responsible for their account, nor are they responsible for yours.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00886

The second group is made up of some of the people of the right. They committed no sin or wrong in this world, and they sought neither power nor corruption on earth. Their consciences were clear, their original nature remained free from the stain of sin, and they were strong in doing good. They too enter Paradise without an account. God says, “We will make the home of the Hereafter for those who seek neither power nor corruption on earth. The happy ending belongs to the Godfearing.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00887

The third group has simple, unformed souls, and their records bear no trace of either good or bad deeds. They remain open to either possibility. God admits them to Paradise through mercy and grace, without letting the painful punishment touch them. Mercy outweighs anger; a soul that is open to good can receive it if nothing blocks it, and God is generous and kind. God says, “I am not unjust to My servants,” “My mercy has gone ahead of My anger,” and “My mercy embraces all things.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00888

The other class consists, broadly, of those who face punishment. It too contains three groups. The first has no good deeds in its record; these people are complete unbelievers and enter Hell without an account. The second has done some good, but what applies to them is God's words, “Their deeds have come to nothing,” and, “We will turn to whatever deeds they did and make them scattered dust.” The third group is truly subject to an account because its members mixed good deeds with bad ones. This group divides in two.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00889

Some people are examined closely, down to every small detail, because that is how they treated others in this world. They demanded every last part of what was owed to them and showed no leniency in their dealings. They will be treated in the next life as they treated people here. Others feared a bad account and dreaded the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. They will not be examined in every detail at the place of reckoning. How, then, could they be punished and kept in the place of punishment?
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00890
XXIII. Events that take place on the Day of Resurrection
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00891

When the Light of all lights appears, the veils lift and the glory of God's sustaining presence is revealed. The rule of oneness overcomes all multiplicity. The powers that act and cause change grow strong as barriers disappear, abilities that were only potential become active, movements reach their goals, and realities emerge from the hidden places and material coverings that concealed them. Every being returns to its source; everything goes back to its origin; everything incomplete reaches completion. All affairs return to God, as He says, “To God belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth,” and, “To God all affairs return.” No one owns anything except by God's leave. God says, “To whom does all power belong today? To God, the One, the All-Powerful.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00892

When every action is joined to its doer, every branch returns to its root, and everything that receives existence is gathered back to its giver, the stars no longer shine. “When the stars are blotted out”; “when the stars are scattered”; the sun's light fades—“when the sun is folded up”—and the moon's light is erased—“when the moon is darkened.” There is no longer a spatial gap or separation between the light-giver and what receives its light. “The sun and the moon are joined together.” The soul joins with the spirits, and the divide between bodies and spirits disappears. That is why the bodies of the people of Paradise take the form of their souls, like a person and their shadow.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00893

The heavens and earth return to the state they were in before they were separated from their original unity. They return to a state of inward oneness, after having been divided in the natural world. The four elements also become one dark element. There is no sun or bitter cold to be seen there. The mountains, which came from sand, return to their state in the vision of the afterlife. God says, “They ask you about the mountains. Say, ‘My Lord will grind them to dust and leave the earth flat and bare, with no rise or hollow.’” All material elements turn into one Fire, different from the elemental fire we know. All matter becomes a raging sea: “When the seas are set ablaze.” The same is suggested by what God says of Pharaoh's people: “They were drowned, then brought into a Fire.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00894

In short, land and sea join, above and below become one, distances and sizes disappear, and barriers are removed. The veils thin for those in the intermediate world and at the place of gathering, where hidden things are exposed and witnesses stand. People are brought out from behind their veils to the place where secrets are revealed. God says, “Stop them; they must be questioned.” Those freed from the prisons of bodies and spirits turn toward the divine presence: “Then, suddenly, they will rush from their graves toward their Lord.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00895

One of the mystics who witnessed these things says: “When the earth brings out all its burdens, leaving nothing hidden within it, it is brought to the darkness beneath the place of gathering.” God says, “The earth and the mountains will be lifted and crushed in a single blow.” The earth is stretched out like a hide and spread flat, with no rise or hollow. It is called “the awakened plain,” because no one sleeps there. God says, “It will be only one blast, and suddenly they will be awake on the plain.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00896

What lies beneath the inward curve of the sphere of the stars becomes Hell. It is called Hell because of its great depth; in Arabic, a well with a deep bottom may be called a jahnam. The Path is set from the earth upward to the outer surface of the sphere of the stars. Its inward face is the floor of Paradise, since all things of the next life lie within the veils of this world. That is why it is said that the earth of Paradise is the Footstool and its roof is the Throne of the All-Merciful. Scales are set up on the plain of gathering. After the general scale, every person held to account receives a scale suited to their deeds.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00897

In the special scales, records and pages are placed and weighed. In this world, we weigh ideas and arguments with the proper measure so that we can tell sound thought from faulty thought and truth from falsehood. The last thing placed on the scale is a servant's saying, “Praise belongs to God.” The Prophet said, “Praise belongs to God; it fills the scale.” Each person's scale is shaped by their actions, and its weight or lightness depends on them.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00898

Every remembrance and saying is weighed except “There is no god but God.” Every action has an opposite in the world of conflict, but the only opposite of affirming God's oneness is associating a partner with Him. The two cannot be together in one scale. Lasting certainty cannot coexist with its opposite, nor can both take turns in the same place. So nothing can be set against that declaration to balance or outweigh it. This is shown by the report about the man whose records were weighed.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00899

Those who associate partners with God have no scale on that Day, because their good deeds have come to nothing. God says, “We will not set up a scale for them on the Day of Resurrection.” A wall called the Heights is placed between Paradise and Hell. It is a place for those whose two pans balance equally. The recording angels bring the books they wrote in this life. These books contain the actions and words of those held to account, but not the beliefs in their hearts. That is why God says, “Everything they did is written in the records,” not “everything they knew.” The books are hung around their necks or placed in their hands. God says, “Every person has their deeds fastened around their neck. On the Day of Resurrection We will bring out for them an open book: ‘Read your book! Today you are enough to call yourself to account.’” And He says, “Every soul will be repaid in full for what it did. He knows best what they do.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00900

Some receive their book in the right hand, some in the left, and some from behind their backs. These are the people who cast God's Book behind their backs in this world and sold it for a small price. They are the leaders of error. Each person is accompanied by a guide and a witness, whether angel or devil. God says, “Every soul will come with a driver and a witness.” Each soul has powers that move it and powers that perceive. The source of its moving powers is called the driver, whether that source is an angel or a devil; the source of its perceiving powers is called the witness. God also says, “Two receivers sit, one on the right and one on the left. Not a word does a person utter without a watcher ready beside them.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00901

Then God comes upon His Throne, carried by angels, and they set it down on the earth shining with the light of its Lord. God says, “You will see the angels surrounding the Throne, praising their Lord. Judgment will be given between them in truth.” Paradise is on the right of the Throne, and the Fire on the other side. The angels of each heaven arrive in a separate row, apart from the angels of the other heavens and from all others. There are seven rows, with the greatest Spirit at their head.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00902

Then the revealed Books are brought—the Books sent down to the prophets—and set there. God says, “The earth will shine with its Lord's light; the Book will be placed; the prophets and witnesses will be brought; and judgment will be given between them in truth.” Every community gathers with its messenger, both those who believed and those who did not. Individuals and prophets who were not sent with a message are gathered apart from the people. Messengers, unlike the other prophets, lead their communities, and have a special station of their own.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00903

That Day, awe of God fills the hearts of everyone present—humans, angels, and jinn. They speak only in whispers. The veils between God and His servants are lifted. This is the meaning of “the uncovering of the shin,” as in God's words, “On the Day the shin is uncovered, they will be called to bow down.” Everyone, whatever their religion, is called to bow in the familiar act of prostration. Those who bow only from fear or to show off will fall flat on their backs. This prostration makes the scale of the people on the Heights heavier—not because it is a required religious act, as some have thought, since religious duties belong only to this world, but because it is a natural act of submission, done without display or ulterior motive.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00904

As mentioned earlier, mercy has the greater share when a person remains close to their original nature and does not turn away from what is true. They may change only by developing toward greater perfection, in keeping with the way God created them. Hell is brought to the gathering place in the form of an angry camel. “On that Day, Hell will be brought near,” so that people can remember. Everyone present sees it plainly: “Hell will be exposed to all who see.” Its terrifying appearance makes all creatures realize that they are helpless, and they turn to God. If God did not hold it back through mercy, it would burn the heavens and the earth.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00905

Death, which is the destruction of creatures through one side of an opposition, is placed between Paradise—the home of life—and the Fire—the home of ruin—in the form of a black-and-white ram. It is killed with a blade called Yahya, the image of life that will last. At Gabriel's command, the source of life, the spirits give life to bodies by God's leave, so that the truth of eternal life appears: death dies, and life lives. A herald of Truth calls, “People of Paradise, you will live forever and never die. People of the Fire, you will remain forever and never die.” Their life is mixed with death, as God says, “They will neither die in it nor live.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00906

The people of Hell alone remain in the Fire. This is the Day of Regret, when each group sees the lasting home to which it belongs. When the people of Paradise see Death, they rejoice greatly and say, “May God bless you! You have freed us from the passing world. You were the best visitor to come to us, the best gift God sent.” The Prophet said, “Death is a gift to the believer.” The people of the Fire, who belong only to this world, see Death and panic. “You were the worst visitor to come to us,” they say. “You kept us from the good life and comfort we had.” Then they say, “Perhaps you can kill us now, so we can escape this suffering and pain.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00907

The gates of the Fire are then shut and never opened again. They close over its people, and its parts are pressed together. Its lowest part becomes its highest, and its highest its lowest. People and devils are inside it like pieces of meat in a pot over a great fire, boiling like scalding water. The Fire and all within it turn over and over. “Whenever it dies down, We increase its blaze.” Their skins are changed, and they see Hell with the certainty of sight: “Then you will see it with the eye of certainty.” The people and stones that fuel it are those who have fallen from human life into the condition of stones. This Fire consumes itself, and its parts attack one another. It leaves bones as dust.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00908

This bodily Fire is not the same as the Fire that reaches the hearts. The bodily Fire may die down when the people of punishment sleep, easing their pain for a time. This is one meaning of “Whenever it dies down, We increase its blaze.” The verse also suggests a fire that can grow stronger or weaker. But true Fire cannot be described in this way. It may instead mean that when the fire consuming their bodies dies down through sleep or something similar, the punishment moves inward. They think about their disgrace and the horror of the Day of Resurrection, which is worse than bodily pain. Know that the Resurrection has many stages and places: the Path, the great gathering, receiving the books, setting up the scales, the Heights, and the gates of Paradise and Hell.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00909

As for the public gathering and display, it is like lining up an army so that its actions can be reviewed. All creatures meet in one place. The veils of time and the differences between places are lifted in that world. People who lived at different times and in different places in this world are all present together, in one open space on one day. God says, “The first and the last will all be gathered for the appointed time of a known Day.” The Prophet was asked about God's words, “He will be given an easy account.” He said, “That is the public display.” Whoever is examined closely in their account will be punished. Just as the soldiers in a parade are recognized by their uniforms and clothing, people there are recognized by their faces, their outward signs, and the forms of their intentions and character, as explained earlier. “The guilty will be recognized by their marks,” and seized by their forelocks and feet, like captives and animals here.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00910

As for the books, the one who receives their book in the right hand will have an easy account and return happily to their people. This is the faithful and blessed person, because the book of their soul belongs to the highest tablets and honored, exalted records. The one who receives their book in the left hand is a hypocrite and wretched, because their book belongs to low records and mistaken, physical writings that can be burned. God says, “The record of the wicked is in Sijjin.” The unbeliever, however, has no book. A hypocrite had the capacity to believe, so they were asked to accept faith and their outward submission was accepted, as it was for ordinary Muslims. But God says of them, “They did not believe in God, the Great.” This includes those who deny God, those who associate partners with Him, and those who arrogantly reject Him. The hypocrite's inner state is one of these three. The outward form of Islam does not help them as it helps the weak and ordinary believers, for the reason explained above.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00911

Those given their book from behind their backs are the ones who cast the Book behind them and sold it for a small price. On the Day of Resurrection they are told, “Take it from behind your back”—from the place where they cast it during their worldly life. This is like the words, “Go back and look for your light.” The book they threw away was the revelation sent to them through the Messenger, not their record of deeds. When they rejected it, they were certain they would never return to God.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00912

The scales have already been explained as far as we could explain their true meaning. The Path is the road to Paradise. It widens for some and narrows for others. In this world it is a meaning; in the next it has a visible form. Some people walk the straight path, while others turn away from it toward the road to Hell. God says, “This is My straight path, so follow it. Do not follow other paths, or they will separate you from His path.” When the Prophet recited this verse, he drew one straight line and several other lines beside it. The straight one is the path of affirming God's oneness, followed by all the prophets and their followers. The crooked lines are the ways of those led astray and the followers of Satan.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00913

A hypocrite has no footing on the path of affirming God's oneness, but does have a footing on the path of existence. Someone who denies the Creator has no footing on the path of existence as a human being, but only as an animal or creature. God says, “There is no creature whose forelock He does not hold.” Even a Muslim who sins will not remain in Hell forever. They may be held on the Path and questioned or punished there, on its surface above Hell, hidden within it. The hooks on the Path hold people there. Since the Path is over the Fire and there is no way to Paradise except across it, God says, “There is not one of you who will not pass over it; this is a decree your Lord must fulfill.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00914

The hooks and barbs described in reports are the image of a person's ties to this world and the worldly restraints that stop them from following the way of truth. On the Day of Resurrection, these ties hold them on the Path. Their faith and the light of their affirmation of God's oneness keep them from falling into the Fire until the intercession of those whom the All-Merciful allows reaches them. Whoever gets past this here will be spared there. If someone gives a debtor more time, God will give them more time. If someone forgives another, God will forgive them. If someone demands their full due here without leniency, God will demand their full due there. If someone treats this community harshly, God will treat them harshly. As the report says, “Your actions will return to you.” So hold fast to noble character. God will treat you as you treat His servants.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00915

As for the Heights, they are a wall between Paradise and Hell. The side facing Paradise has a door, and mercy lies within it; its outer side faces Hell, and punishment lies there. Those whose scales are equal stand on it. They look toward Paradise with one eye and toward Hell with the other, but neither side outweighs the other enough for them to enter one of the two places. God says, “On the Heights are people who recognize each group by its marks.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00916

There is another interpretation of the Heights and its people, and careful thought shows that it is close to the one just given. While they remain in this natural life, the state of fully realized mystics resembles the afterlife state of those whose good and bad deeds balance. Their knowledge and insight, and the thinness of the veil around their bodies, nearly give them the joy of Paradise. But their dense physical bodies and their continued earthly life keep them from complete union and spiritual fulfillment. They occupy a middle state. Yet their essential nature and high souls stand in an elevated place. In Arabic, “the Heights” is a plural form meaning high places. A high place can see more clearly than a lower one, just as the crest of a horse or a rooster is high.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00917

Commentators have offered two readings. Most say the Heights are the upper edge of the wall between Paradise and Hell. This is reported from Ibn Abbas, who also said that the Heights are the raised part of the Path. Hasan and al-Zajjaj offer another reading: “On the Heights” means “among those who know the people of Paradise and Hell.” The verse means that some people recognize both groups by their marks. When Hasan was told that these were people whose good and bad deeds were equal, he struck his cheek and said, “They are people God has placed where they can recognize the people of Paradise and the people of Hell.” He then added, “By God, I do not know—perhaps some of them are with us.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00918

Those who follow the first reading disagree about who stands on the Heights. Some say they are the nobles and the most obedient people; others say they are angels who recognize the people of both abodes; others say they are prophets, whom God seats on the wall to distinguish them from the rest and let them see the people of Paradise and Hell and the degrees of their reward and punishment. Another view says they are people at the lowest rank of the rewarded. A fifth says they are martyrs. That last view is mistaken: the verse says that they recognize both the blessed and the wretched, but a martyr does not necessarily have this knowledge. If “recognize” only meant that the people of Paradise have smiling faces and the people of Hell dark faces and blue eyes, everyone at the Resurrection would know that, so it would not set the people of the Heights apart. The view that they are people of the lowest rank also fails, since they would not have the knowledge described. The second view fails because the verse calls them men, a word that usually distinguishes men from women; angels are neither. So “they recognize them by their marks” most likely means that, in this world, they recognized people of faith and goodness, and people of evil and rebellion. God places them on high stations suited to their rank, where they can see all people and testify about them. They know that the people of reward have reached their stations and the people of punishment have reached theirs.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00919
Someone may object: the verse says that they have not entered Paradise, though they hope to do so. That does not suit the prophets or people like them.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00920

We reply: their not entering Paradise at the outset does not lessen their honor or the height of their rank. As for the statement that they hope to enter it, hope here means certainty. God reports Abraham as saying, “And I hope that He will forgive my fault on the Day of Judgment.” There can be no doubt that his hope here expresses certainty. The same is true in this passage.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00921

In short, the description of the people on the Heights points to a great honor. They sit in a lofty place and recognize both groups by their marks. Such a distinction belongs to people of high standing, not to people whose good and bad deeds happen to balance. The stronger view, therefore, is that the people on the Heights hold an exalted rank.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00922

This is supported by a report transmitted by Muhammad ibn Ya'qub al-Kulayni. Ibn al-Kawwa' asked Ali about God's words, “On the Heights are people who recognize each group by its marks.” Ali replied, “We are on the Heights. We recognize our supporters by their marks. We are the Heights, through knowledge of whom alone God is known. No one enters Paradise unless we recognize him, and no one enters the Fire unless he rejects us.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00923

These are some of the events of the Day of Resurrection. Many reports describe that Day, and scholars have recorded them in books. We have explained some of them as far as our strength and ability allow. The key to this knowledge is knowing the soul, for it brings forth and receives the realities of the next life. In truth, the soul is the Path, the Book, the Scale, the Heights, Paradise, and Hell, as reports from our Imams indicate.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00924

Ibn Babawayh relates in Meanings of the Reports and The Book of Divine Unity that Ja'far al-Sadiq was asked about the straight path. He replied, “It is the Commander of the Faithful.” Ali ibn al-Husayn, the master of worshippers, said, “We are God's gates, and we are the straight path.” Ja'far ibn Muhammad said that God's words, “The path of those You have blessed,” refer to Muhammad and his descendants.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00925

Hisham ibn Salim also reports that he asked Ja'far al-Sadiq about the words, “We shall set up the just scales for the Day of Resurrection, and no soul will be wronged in anything.” He replied, “They are the prophets and their appointed successors.” And the Book mentioned in the verses about the record of the righteous in Illiyyin and the record of the wicked in Sijjin means the souls of the righteous and of the wicked, as explained earlier.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00926

Ali also said, “You are the clear Book, whose signs reveal what lies hidden,” and, “Your cure is within you, though you do not see it; your illness comes from you, though you do not notice it.” These sayings show that the human soul is where the joys of Paradise and the pains and punishments of Hell take place.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00927
XXIV. What Paradise and Hell are
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00928

Paradise, as described in the Book and the teachings of the Prophet, and as confirmed by reason and spiritual insight, is the home of lasting life and peace. There is no death, aging, sickness, grief, worry, decay, or loss there. It is the home of rest and honor. Its people feel no weariness or fatigue. They have whatever their souls desire and whatever delights their eyes, and they remain there forever. Its people are God's neighbors, His friends and beloved ones, and those honored by Him.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00929

They enjoy different kinds of blessing and stand at different ranks. Some take pleasure in praising, honoring, and magnifying God among the angels brought near to Him. Others enjoy the pleasures of the senses: kinds of food, drink, and fruit; couches and cushions; marriage with the wide-eyed companions; service from youths who remain young; sitting on soft cushions and rugs; and wearing fine green silk and brocade. Each person enjoys what they desire and seek, according to the aim of their soul. In general, things in the Gardens begin from acts of knowing and from powers that bring things into being. Matter and the causes that receive and support material things have no role there. Things in that world exist as forms without matter, movement, passivity, change, or transition.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00930

Hell is the home of its people, where they face disgrace, sickness, grief, pain, hunger, thirst, renewed punishment, and changing skins. They neither die nor truly live. Their punishment is not ended by death, and it is not eased for them. The true people of Hell are those who reject God and associate partners with Him; their faces are dark. People from among those who affirm God's oneness but have sinned are taken out of Hell through mercy and intercession.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00931

A report from our Imams says that people who affirm God's oneness feel no pain in the Fire when they first enter it; God gives them pain when they leave it. This fits our reasoning. A person who knows God's oneness has a soul lit by truth and certainty, lifted from the lower world toward the higher one. The Fire does not enter the place where knowledge and faith are. As the report says, “The Fire does not consume the place of faith.” In truth, the people of Hell are the unbelievers and those who associate partners with God. They will taste no coolness or drink there, except scalding water and foul fluid. If they ask for food, they are given the fruit of the tree of Zaqqum; if they cry for help, they receive water like molten metal that burns their faces. What a terrible drink and resting place! They call out from far away, but are told, “Be driven away, and do not speak to Me.” They call, “Malik, let your Lord put an end to us,” and he says, “You will remain here.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00932

You must know that the Garden from which Adam and his wife were sent out because of their mistake—the Garden of spirits, which people of knowledge and religion call the place of the covenant and the source from which human descendants were taken—is not the same as the Garden promised to the Godfearing. That promised Garden is the Garden of the intermediate world. No one reaches it until their worldly life ends in death. All people reach it only after this world is destroyed, the heavens and earth pass away, and all movements reach their goals. The two Gardens agree in their true nature and level of being, because both are homes of life in its own right and of knowing through images. Neither undergoes change, decay, interruption, opposition, or conflict.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00933

The beginnings and goals of existence face one another in a pattern of return. As you have learned, death begins the human soul's journey back to God, while natural life is the end of its descent from Him. The sages and mystics compare these two descending and ascending series to the two halves of a circle. This shows that the soul's returning journey bends back toward its source; it does not travel along the same route as its descent. Each rank on the upward curve corresponds to a rank on the downward curve, though the two ranks are not identical.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00934

Know also that there are two Gardens: a Garden we can sense and a Garden we can understand with the intellect. God says, “For whoever fears standing before their Lord there are two Gardens,” and, “In them are two of every kind of fruit.” In the general study of existence, you have learned that there is an intellectual world containing intellectual forms and luminous patterns that match all the lights in the outer world. You have also learned that there is a world of images that can be sensed but have no material basis, even though they have direction and location. The Garden we can sense belongs to the people of the right; the intellectual Garden belongs to those brought near to God, the people of the highest realm.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00935

There are also two Hells: one we can sense and one that is inward. The visible Fire belongs to unbelievers; the inward Fire belongs to hypocrites and the arrogant. One burns bodies; the other burns hearts. Each visible Garden and Hell is a world of forms. One is an image of God's mercy, the other an image of His anger. God says, “Whoever is overtaken by My anger has fallen.” Just as mercy is part of God's own being and anger arises as a response, reason shows—and God's words support—that mercy came before anger. “My mercy has gone ahead of My anger,” and “My mercy embraces all things.” In the same way, Paradise was created as an end in itself, while Hell exists as a secondary result. There is a secret in this.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00936

You have learned that the next life does not occupy a place in this world, either above or below it. Everything that occupies a place in this world changes, decays, and passes away. Whatever is like this belongs to this world. The next life is the final home, not a home of ruin. It lies within this world, behind the veils of the heavens and earth, like a child in its mother's womb. Yet Paradise and Hell each have places in this world that act as mirrors and signs of their partial forms.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00937

This is how we should understand the reports that place Paradise or Hell in particular locations. The Prophet said, “The space between my grave and my pulpit is one of the gardens of Paradise.” Another report says, “The believer's grave is one of the gardens of Paradise, and the hypocrite's grave is one of the pits of the Fire.” It is also reported that a spring from Paradise is on Mount Arvand. Abu Ja'far said that God created a Garden in the west, from which this Euphrates flows. The spirits of believers leave their graves every evening and morning, fall upon its fruits, eat, enjoy its blessings, and meet and recognize one another. When dawn comes, they rise from the Garden and fly through the air between earth and sky. When the sun rises, they return to their graves.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00938

God also created a Fire in the east for the spirits of unbelievers. At night, they eat from its Zaqqum and drink its scalding water. At dawn, they go to a valley in Yemen called Barahut, hotter than the fires of this world, where they meet and recognize one another. In the evening, they return to the Fire. This continues until the Day of Resurrection.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00939

In Al-Kafi, Abu Basir reports that he said to Abu Abd Allah: “We have heard that the spirits of believers are in the crops of green birds, grazing in Paradise and resting in lamps beneath the Throne.” He replied, “No, they are not in the crops of birds.” Abu Basir asked, “Where are they, then?” He said, “In a Garden shaped like their bodies in Paradise.” The same book reports that the Prophet said, “The worst Jews are the Jews of Banan; the worst Christians are the Christians of Najran; and the worst water on earth is the water of Barahut, a valley in Hadramawt. The skulls and remains of unbelievers go there.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00940

Many reports place Paradise in the heavens. Mujahid says that God's words, “In heaven is your provision and what you are promised,” refer to Paradise and Hell; al-Dahhak says the same. It is reported that Abd Allah ibn Salam said, “The noblest of God's creation is Abu al-Qasim,” meaning the Prophet, “and Paradise is in the heavens.” Most say it is in the seventh heaven. Ibn Abbas is reported to have said that it is above the seven heavens, while Hell lies beneath layers of seas.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00941

This is supported by the established report of the Prophet's night journey, which says that the Lote Tree was in the seventh heaven. The Qur'an says, “He saw him once more at the Lote Tree of the furthest boundary, beside which is the Garden of Refuge.” Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud is reported to have said that Paradise is in the fourth heaven, and that God will place it wherever He wills on the Day of Resurrection. Abd Allah ibn Umar is reported to have said that Paradise is folded up and hangs from the horns of the sun, and that the spirits of believers are in birds like sparrows. They recognize one another by the fruit of Paradise. A similar idea appears in the words of some ancient sages, who said that spirits descend into this world from the rays of the sun.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00942

Some reports place Paradise in the lowest heaven. In the account of the Prophet's night journey, he saw Adam, the father of humanity, in the lowest heaven. On Adam's right was a door from which a pleasant breeze came; on his left was a door from which came a foul breeze. Gabriel told him that one was Paradise and the other Hell.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00943

Other reports place it in one of the valleys of the earth. The Prophet is said to have reached a cool, pleasant valley on the way to Jerusalem and heard a voice. Gabriel told him, “That is the voice of Paradise.” Other reports say that Paradise and Hell appeared on earth at certain times. During an eclipse prayer, the Prophet said, “There is nothing you have been promised that I have not seen in this prayer. The Fire was brought near.” This was when people saw him step back, afraid its heat might reach him. He continued, “Then Paradise was brought near. That was when you saw me step forward and stand in my place. I reached out my hand, wanting to take some of its fruit so that you could see it, then I decided not to.” Muslim recorded this report.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00944

Some say that when the Prophet saw Hell during the eclipse prayer, he shielded his face from its heat with his hand and clothing, stepped back, and pleaded, “Did You not promise me, my Lord, that You would not punish them while I am among them?”—referring to God's words, “God would not punish them while you are among them, nor would He punish them while they seek forgiveness.” It is also reported that one day, after praying, the Prophet climbed the pulpit and pointed toward the front of the mosque. He said, “I have just seen Paradise and Hell, as if they were placed on this wall. I have never seen good and evil like I have today.” Al-Bukhari recorded this report. Most people say that Hell is beneath the seventh earth.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00945

Other reports place Hell in the heavens. We have already quoted Mujahid and al-Dahhak on God's words, “In heaven is your provision and what you are promised.” In the report of the Prophet's night journey, he saw Malik, the guardian of Hell, in the lowest heaven. A path into Hell was opened for him, and he looked down into it until its smoke and sparks rose up to him from the door on his left.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00946

Other reports place Hell in the sea. Ali is reported to have asked a Jew, “Where is the Fire in your Book?” He answered, “In the sea.” Ali said, “I think he is right,” because God says, “By the sea set ablaze.” Commentaries also say that the sea set ablaze is the Fire. Ahmad ibn Hanbal reports that the Prophet said, “The sea is Hell.” Abd Allah ibn Umar reports that the Prophet said, “No one should travel by sea except to fight in God's way or to make pilgrimage, for beneath the sea is a Fire,” or, “beneath the Fire is a sea.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00947

Al-Tha'labi reports the Prophet's words, “The sea is a Fire within a Fire.” Ibn Abbas is reported to have said that Hell lies beneath a sea called Qays, beyond which is the sea called the Deaf Sea, beyond that the Covered Sea, then the Sea of Marmas, then the Still Sea, and then the Weeping Sea, the last of the seas and the one that surrounds them all. Each of these seas surrounds the one before it. Some early authorities explain God's words, “They ask you to hasten the punishment, though Hell surrounds the unbelievers,” by saying that Hell is the sea surrounding them. The stars are scattered into it, then it is kindled and becomes Hell.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00948

Al-Dahhak explains God's words about Noah's people, “They were drowned, then brought into a Fire,” by saying that both happened at once in this world: they drowned on one side and burned on the other. This is like the earlier report from the sage Socrates that people who commit grave sins are thrown into Tartarus. The translator explains that Tartarus is a great cleft, a deep place into which rivers flow, meaning the sea or a deep whirlpool.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00949

Other reports point to the Fire being in this very land, like the report about the valley mentioned earlier. Some say that part of Hell is on earth. Qatada explains God's words, “Was the one who built his building on the edge of a collapsing bank, which then collapsed into the Fire of Hell,” by saying, “By God, what is falling into Hell if not that?” Jabir ibn Abd Allah is reported to have said, “I saw smoke rising from the land of Darara.” Some say that Hadramawt is part of that region. This is close to the report about the valley of Barahut, which Ali described as the place God hates most. It contains the spirits of unbelievers and a well of foul black water where they stay. A man said that he spent a night in the valley and heard someone calling, “Dumah!” all night. He told a scholar, who said that Dumah was the name of the angel in charge of the spirits of unbelievers.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00950

Al-Asma'i reports a man from Hadramawt as saying that a terrible, foul smell comes from the direction of Barahut, after which news arrives that a great unbeliever has died. Some of these reports speak of the spirits of unbelievers, without mentioning the Fire. But when we consider them together with the other reports and with God's words, “They are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, and when the Hour comes, ‘Bring Pharaoh's people into the harshest punishment,’” the connection to the Fire becomes clearer.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00951
1. A note on these reports
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00952

To people who rely on outward readings, these reports may seem to contradict one another. To those who have reached spiritual insight, their inward meanings agree. Their knowledge rests on sound proofs and clear insight. They are as certain of these truths as they are of the sun at midday. Others, who rely on debate or repeat reports without understanding them, find the claims contradictory because they have not entered a subject through its proper door.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00953

As you have learned, Paradise and Hell belong to another state of being and another world. Its beings are forms without matter, passivity, movement, or change. Everything in this world is created, corrupted, renewed, and passing away, with a place and direction. So, when a report places Paradise or Hell in a location in this world, it may mean that they are inwardly present in that place. When people say that Paradise is in the seventh heaven and Hell is beneath the heavens, they do not mean that Paradise is physically inside the heavenly sphere. They mean it is there in an inward way, as the soul is within the body. The same applies to Hell.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00954

You have also learned that Paradise and Hell are to this world as a child is to the womb. The next life remains hidden until this world ends; the outward structure must fall before the inward world is fully revealed. Another meaning is that some places in this world act as mirrors that reveal particular forms of Paradise or Hell. A mirror shows a physical image, but the image is not inside the mirror. In the same way, some places show the forms of Paradise or Hell to those with spiritual insight. The space between the Prophet's grave and pulpit is one such mirror; a person with insight can see in it a garden of Paradise. The Prophet's mosque wall, the Euphrates, a spring on Mount Arvand, the valley of Barahut, and other places can also reveal forms of Paradise or Hell.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00955

The sea mentioned in the report is not the visible sea. It means another, inward sea that the senses cannot perceive, as in God's words, “By the sea set ablaze.” The seven seas mentioned by Ibn Abbas and Ka'b al-Ahbar, or the Fire beneath seven seas, do not mean the seas of this world. They mean the levels of nature in their basic being. Nature itself is an unseen Fire: it burns bodies, melts forms, and changes skins.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00956
XXV. Signs and forms of Paradise and Hell
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00957

Know that every real kind of thing and every basic meaning has a universal reality, particular examples, and physical forms that appear in this world. A human being, for example, has a universal reality: the universal human intellect, which gathers all human qualities and features in a higher and nobler way. This is the spirit God refers to when He says, “I breathed into him of My spirit.” There are also particular examples, such as Zayd and Amr, and visible forms, like images in mirrors or polished bodies.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00958

Paradise has the same kinds of forms. Its universal reality is the spirit of the world and a sign of God's name, the All-Merciful. God says, “We will gather the Godfearing before the All-Merciful as honored guests.” Its universal image is like the Greatest Throne, the place where the All-Merciful is established. Its particular examples include the hearts of believers, since “the believer's heart is God's Throne.” It also has visible forms in this world, such as the spring mentioned in the reports from Mount Arvand.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00959

Hell also has a universal reality, shared by all its particular forms: distance from nearness to God and from His mercy. This is tied to His names the Compeller, the Avenger, and the All-Overpowering. Hell has a universal world of images, with seven levels beneath the Footstool. The Footstool is where the two feet are placed: the foot of the Compeller, which presses down on the people of Hell, and the foot of truth, which stands firm with God and belongs to the people of Paradise. There are roots of the lote tree there, which is the tree of Zaqqum, food for sinners. That is where the deeds of the wicked and hypocrites come to an end.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00960

Hell also has particular examples: each person's nature is the source of bodily suffering, and their soul and desires are the source of spiritual suffering. It has visible forms and places in this world, as in the reports about the valley of Barahut and other places. Paradise and Hell also have gates, as we will explain.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00961
XXVI. The gates of Paradise and Hell
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00962

The gates of Paradise are mentioned in God's words, “The angels will enter to them from every gate,” and, “The gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise,” and, “Gardens of lasting life, whose gates are open to them.” The gates of Hell are mentioned in, “Enter the gates of Hell, where you will remain,” “When they come to it, its gates will be opened,” and, “It has seven gates, and each gate has an assigned share of them.”
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00963

There is disagreement about what these gates are. Some say they are the seven powers of perception in a human being: the five senses and two inner powers, imagination and estimation. One perceives images; the other perceives particular meanings. These gates lead into Hell, but they also lead into Paradise when a person uses them for worship, good deeds, and understanding general truths through particular, sensory things. In short, they become gates to Paradise when used for the purpose for which they were created. Paradise also has an eighth gate, which is the heart.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00964

Others say that the gates are the seven bodily parts subject to religious duties. Another view is that the gates of Hell are seven bad qualities, such as envy, stinginess, and pride, while the gates of Paradise are their good opposites, such as knowledge, generosity, and courage. It is possible that there are seven main kinds of bad qualities, each with many branches, and eight main kinds of good qualities, each with its own kinds, as described in books about character. But the first view is the best and fits the argument most closely.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00965

Each of the seven senses can be a gate to worldly desires, which become burning fires and painful traits for the soul in the next life. But if a person uses these senses for good, they become gates to knowledge of reality, to understanding, and to good deeds. Through these, the person is rewarded, rises to the spiritual realm, and enters Paradise with the ranks of angels. Each sense has an outer side and an inner side. Its inner side opens toward mercy; its outer side faces punishment. The outer side opens toward Hell, or toward what makes a person deserve to enter it. The inner side opens toward Paradise, or toward what makes a person deserve to enter it.
Book Eleven: Bodily resurrection and the states of the afterlife
passage-en-00966

When the gates of Hell are closed, the gates of Paradise are opened. They are like a door that opens into one room while closing off another: closing one set of gates is the same as opening the other. The exception is the gate of the heart, the eighth gate. It is always closed to those who are completely veiled from truth and reject faith, and open only to people of faith and knowledge.
